extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, researchers, and policymakers interested in U.S. financial history and bank/thrift regulation
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the U.S. savings and loan (S&L) crisis of the 1980s–1990s covering causes, regulatory changes, failures, prosecutions, and policy responses. Useful as a background reference on thrift regulation, insolvency metrics, and legislative remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation Q deposit interest caps
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal regulations, especially Regulation Q, placed caps on deposit interest rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caps encouraged depositors to move funds into money market mutual funds; the resulting outflows pressured thrifts and helped prompt the Depository Institutions Deregulation and Monetary Control Act of 1980 which phased out Reg Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit insurance limit (40,000 → 100,000)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposit insurance limit was raised from $40,000 to $100,000 per account by the Depository Institutions Deregulation and Monetary Control Act of 1980.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raised to bolster depositor confidence as part of wider deregulation reforms; affected depositor behavior and thrift risk management incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded thrift lending powers (construction, commercial, lines of credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation (notably Garn–St. Germain and the 1980 Act) expanded thrift lending powers to include construction loans, commercial real estate lending, and lines of credit, and allowed adjustable-rate mortgages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to diversify thrift portfolios but was not matched by increased supervision; many thrifts concentrated risky lending geographically and in unfamiliar asset classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net worth / capital requirement changes (e.g., 5% → 3%)
rubrics_metrics.description: FHLBB lowered net worth requirements from five percent in 1980 to three percent in 1982; phase-in rules and rules for new institutions allowed even lower effective requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted extreme leverage (examples cited such as $2M capital to $1.3B assets), increasing fragility and susceptibility to market shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory forbearance policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Forbearance: regulators chose not to apply regulations that would normally disrupt bank operation, allowing insolvent or thinly capitalized thrifts to remain open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbearance delayed closures and exposed the deposit insurer (FSLIC) to mounting losses; political pressure and concerns about depositor panic drove forbearance decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissive accounting rules (supervisory goodwill / deferred loss reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of regulatory accounting principles permitted institutions to defer reporting of losses and to treat certain intangibles (supervisory goodwill) as capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules masked true capital shortfalls, reduced triggers for supervisory intervention, and facilitated purchases of insolvent thrifts using accounting constructs rather than cash recapitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net worth certificates and FSLIC recapitalization authority (Garn–St. Germain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Garn–St. Germain allowed the FSLIC to provide direct capital injections through 'net worth certificates' as a means to support weak thrifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided short-term relief but also encouraged risk-taking by substituting insurer support for market discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: CEBA 1987 closure criteria (equity ratio > 0.5%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Competitive Equality Banking Act of 1987 included a provision that thrift supervisors were not to close thrifts that had equity ratios of more than 0.5 percent and that otherwise met lax viability criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory constraint limited supervisory closures, contributing to moral hazard and allowing risky institutions to continue operating.

rubrics_metrics.name: FIRREA 1989 capital and supervisory reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: The Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act of 1989 (FIRREA) dissolved the FHLBB and FSLIC, created the Resolution Trust Corporation (RTC), removed intangibles like goodwill from regulatory capital, doubled minimum capital to six percent within two years, applied risk-based capital rules to thrifts, and re-imposed restrictions on non-residential mortgage portfolios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FIRREA tightened capital and supervisory standards, funded financial-crime prosecutions, and set the institutional framework (RTC, OTS, FDIC role changes) to wind down insolvent thrifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: RTC asset disposition and conservatorship policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Resolution Trust Corporation sold or liquidated insolvent thrifts under conservatorship and was authorized to sell assets in small tranches over generous time periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selling in small tranches made assets more marketable and helped the RTC recover a substantial portion of book value while avoiding large market disruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDIC Improvement Act supervisory requirements and prompt corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: The FDIC Improvement Act of 1991 expanded examination authority (requiring annual inspections and sufficient exam staff) and provided federal agencies with prompt corrective action powers to compel recapitalization and to take remedial steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powers included suspending certain business activities, banning dividends, replacing directors, and imposing a 'hard stop' (banks below minimum capital could remain open only up to 90 days before receivership).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insolvency metric: tangible capital to assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Insolvency of thrifts was measured on a tangible capital to assets basis (excluding intangibles), which could differ markedly from regulatory capital measures used by FHLBB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible-capital metrics revealed a larger number of insolvent institutions when intangibles were excluded, informing policy decisions to wind down institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-crisis criminal enforcement (Crime Control Act 1990)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crime Control Act of 1990 established a special counsel to investigate and prosecute fraud in financial institutions; DOJ prosecutions between 1988–1992 produced many convictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While fraud occurred in a minority of failures by many estimates, enhanced criminal enforcement aimed to deter and punish insider abuse and control fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions (attempted) on brokered deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: FSLIC sought to restrict thrifts' use of brokered deposits, which regulators viewed as fueling rapid thrift growth, though some restrictions were struck down by courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory attempts to limit brokered deposits were part of efforts to slow growth and constrain asset-liability mismatches, but legal challenges limited enforcement.
